Thanks! Indeed, the amount of information required to follow the NEs predicted by our model varies across rules. For example, in the case of zero delivery costs:


**BasicAV**: If there is no upper bound on the cost of the projects, one may simply request the full budget amount. If a project gets most votes it takes everything, and otherwise its cost is irrelevant.


**AV/cost**: It suffices to know the proportion of the votes that a project gets.


**Phragmen**: For plurality ballots, it suffices to act as in the case of AV/cost. For party-list ballots we require the same information + the size of our party. For the general case, we need full information about the votes (as an NE may not even exist).


**MES-cost**: The most approved project can choose its cost based only on the proportion of approvals it gets, and the expected number of voters. The second most-approved project additionally needs to know how many of its voters also support the first most-approved project, and so on. So the less popular a project is, the more difficult it is for it to follow an NE.


**MES-apr**: In general, we need full information.


Note that the above describes the information needed to ensure that it is possible to implement an NE for every possible preference profile. In the response to reviewer aPJA, we have argued that in practice (as indicated by our experiments), it typically suffices to know the proportion of approvals a project expects to get.

The assumption of full information can be seen as an approximation of the voters' actual beliefs, which guide their strategic choices. While perfect information is rarely attainable, project proposers may still form reasonably accurate predictions about which projects will be submitted and how votes will be distributed—based on trends and outcomes from previous editions of participatory budgeting in the same municipality.

Indeed, we observe that different methods incentivize setting larger or smaller project prices, depending on what voting rule we are using. Let us make a few comments, depending on the voting rule.

BasicAV:

1. As we indicated in the introduction, in Wroclaw, Poland, PB elections we observe that proposers choose the costs strategically, in the way suggested by our model. Namely, they choose very high prices, close to the highest allowed cost.
2. In Poznan, Poland, in each of the years 2023, 2024, 2025 there is a project submitted by, in essence, the same proposer, with common name "Trener osiedlowy, trener senioralny, ....". This project always has many more votes than any other project and requests almost the entire budget, as our NE predicts (it had won in each of these cases). In years 2023 and 2024 this is the unique winning project. In 2025, apparently, Poznan imposed an upper bound of 2M PLN on the cost of a single project, but set the budget to be 3M PLN. The second winning project seems to have guessed that "Trener osiedlowy, trener senioralny, ... " would ask for 2M PLN and would get the highest number of votes, so it requested 1M PLN, to win the remaining money. If our model included an upper bound on the cost of a project, in NE it would predict that project with the second highest number of votes should request as much as there would be left after the most popular project took its share (modulo the upper bound on the cost, in which case the third project could also ask for some money, and so on) 
3. In Zabrze, Poland, in years 2020 and 2021 (we did not see data for other years) almost all projects requested full or nearly full budget, as predicted by our model.



MES-cost:

In case of MES-cost, there are only a few real-life applications. Indeed, the only one that is close to the model from the paper is the “Green Million” PB election from Wieliczka. In particular, our model allows each voter to approve as many projects as he or she chooses. Similarly, there were no constraints in Wieliczka. In effect, about half of the voters approved only a single project. The tendency to vote for a single project makes predictions about equilibrium project costs particularly easy, since project proposers only need to get a rough idea of the proportion of approvals they would receive to choose costs as in the NE.

Other rules:

For Phragmen, AV/cost, and MES-Apr there are essentially no real-life examples of their usage. Hence, we would say that the NE analysis suggests that under these models one should aim for costs that are proportional to expected number of approvals (indeed, our experimental results suggest that the three rules would give similar outcomes, so one can follow the suggestions given by AV/cost, as they are simplest to implement). Hence, following an approximation of an NE would be relatively easy---the proposers would simply have to get an idea of the proportion of approvals their projects are likely to get.

Note that the proposers' proportional strategy---to request funds proportional to the expected number of approvals---seems to work for MES-cost, as well as Phragmen, AV/cost, and MES-Apr. This seems to be a consequence of the fact that voters behave differently under MES-cost (where they largely focus on single proects, so the proportional strategy approximately implemetns MES-cost NE) and differently for the three latter rules (where it implements AV/cost NE, which--given our experimental results---in practice is closely related to NEs for Phragmen and MES-Apr)

Finally, we stress that the assumption of full information allows for a clear-cut analysis of the model, which lets us pinpoint tendencies in project proposers’ behavior. It is common for theoretical models to simplify reality in order to uncover key insights.

rebuttal.value:
REVIEWER'S COMMENT


1. It remains unclear to me whether a 100% percent sure Ground Truth versus a partial knowledge /noisy signal makes a different in the existence of equilibria.

ANSWER: See answer to Question 1.



QUESTIONS


1. How will exact ground truth / noisy information on voters' preferences affect the existence of an equilibrium? Do you at least have some guesses or conjectures?

ANSWER: We conjecture that the noise in the information can have a strong impact on the equilibria, especially regarding the complexity of their computation. In particular, noise and partial information would require different equilibrium notions, possibly relaxed in some ways. We suspect that there are variants of partial information setting that would maintain many of our results (e.g., if the votes come from some known distribution), but we are quite certain that one can come up with definitions under which equilibria disappear completely. Nevertheless, we leave the answer to this question as a compelling direction for future research.

2. In remark 2.1, you mentioned that you complement MES by Phragmen rules to use up the budget as much as possible. Will this complementary process affect the equilibrium?

ANSWER: In a typical setting, the MES-cost completion does not matter, because under NE MES-cost is exhaustive: Each project requests the full endowment from the voters that approve it (and did not yet spend their money on projects considered in previous iterations). The NE may not be exhaustive either if some voters do not approve any projects---which is very unlikely---or when a project's delivery cost is higher than the endowment held by the voters at the time when a given project is considered. In this latter case, the completion method can, indeed, affect the equilibrium (but one could also argue that in such a setting the project would withdraw, as it would have no chance of funding, and we would be back to an exhaustive equilibrium; that goes beyond our model, though).


3. In the second paragraph of the intro, there are sentences like "Among 25% instances, half of them XXX; in another 50%, more than 30% YYY". This kind of expression looks counterintuitive to me. Why not count the properties based on the whole dataset?

ANSWER: These sentences look somewhat complicated because we compute fractions of three types. The first percentage regards the number of PB instance (in Wroclaw or in Pabulib overall), the second percentage refers to the number of projects within these PB instances, and the final percentage refers to the cost of these projects, as a fraction of the highest allowed cost. We will look for ways to express these statistics in a clearer way.

4. I would like to hear more potential applications or insights this paper could give on future research or voting practices.

ANSWER: As far as insights go, we find the following three to be most important:

a) MES-cost leads to very different equilibria than MES-Apr (which, on the other hand, leads to similar resutls to Phragmen). Specifically, MES-cost leads to funding fewer, more expensive projects. This is important for city officials as handling fewer projects is easier logistically. In particular, we would suggest that if one wanted to focus on only a single MES variant, then looking at MES-cost is more appealing than looking at MES-apr. 

b) Looking at the Pabulib instances, typically projects undershoot their costs (in the sense that under a best response they could request significantly more, provided they would not discourage voters from supporting them). This means that, typically, proposers should focus on designing the best, most appealing projects, without overly worrying about the costs.

c) Since MES-cost is typically exhaustive under an equilibrium, it might be interesting to see how the assumption on choosing equilibrium costs affects the complexity of various problems. For example, deciding if there is a tie under MES is NP-complete (L. Janeczko, P. Faliszewski, Ties in Multiwinner Approval Voting, IJCAI 2023) but does it remain NP-complete under NE costs?

REVIEWER'S COMMENTS

1. Intuitive explanations of some of the results in the paper will improve its readability, especially in Section 4.4. 

ANSWER: Thank you, we will make sure to clarify the intuition behind our results in the final version!

2. Further weaknesses include a lack of robustness analysis and a lack of practical relevance of the proposed solution in the real world.

ANSWER: The analysis of robustness of equilibria is indeed a good avenue for future research, which is further related to, e.g., our assumptions of perfect knowledge of the players. Regarding the practical relevance of our results, we believe that the strongest value of the paper is in understanding differences between the incentives provided by the rules. In particular, we observe a significant difference between MES-cost and MES-Apr/Phragmen, where the former is guaranteed to have NE, and in experiments selects fewer, more expensive projects. This makes MES-cost a more appealing proportional rule from the perspective of cities---implementing fewer, more expensive projects is logistically easier for them.


QUESTIONS

1. I could not fully understand the end goal here. While equilibrium analysis in the paper is mostly predictive analysis, it will help if the authors comment on the prescriptive angle of the analysis as well. As a proposer deciding how to set project prices, what information do I need for different selection rules, and how realistic is it to obtain and/or process the information?

ANSWER: In general (for exceptions see the answer to comment 5 for reviewer Ewmz), in our setting, a proposer is required to know the approval sets of the voters, projects' delivery costs, and the voting rule (including the tie-breaking rule). We acknowledge that the perfect knowledge assumption is an idealization. However, the voting rule is known from the setup of an election. Further, we assume that an estimation of delivery costs can be made through an analysis of the proposals. Finally, an estimation for voters' ballots can be obtained, e.g., through reliable polls. But, foremost, we view the value of our results to be in the improved understanding of the analyzed rules.


2. Can authors comment on the rules that induce the desired equilibrium point in the Nash strategy (or dominant strategy) profile? In other words, do there exist mechanisms that induce the desired equilibrium outcome?

ANSWER: Thank you for this suggestion! In our work we aimed at understanding the properties of most popular voting rules in the context of strategic cost selection. The mechanism design approach to this problem is of natural interest, but we defer it to future work.

3. The paper lacks robustness studies. How robust are the equilibrium notions to miscalculation by a single or/few agents?

ANSWER: Generally, if some of the proposers submit slightly lower costs than prescribed in an NE, then the remaining ones can either submit slightly higher ones or maintain NE ones without losing too much. If some voters overshoot their costs, then their projects may end up not funded and there might be a very large difference in the results. See also the answer to Comment 2.

REVIEWER'S COMMENTS

1. It's not clear why the player's utility is precisely how much money the project additionally brings. For instance, it could be that the proposers care first and foremost about getting the project funded to the smallest feasible amount, and the extra money after that is far less important – so something akin to the extended utility function of Remark 3.1.

ANSWER: If the proposers only cared about getting the project funded at the minimum cost, then we would miss the strategic interaction---the proposers would simply submit the lowest cost, without regard for what the others do. On the other hand, if their utility improves above the minimal cost in some monotonic way (e.g., a sublinear one, if one is after a slow rate of growth), then this is equivalent to the current setting (see our response to Reviewer Ewmz). As for Remark 3.1., if one likes this approach, then all the results still hold for it. 

2. Secondly, the arguments against cost-interval games in PB (Section 6) sees not very convincing as well. I think your example of “voter approves building a bike path for at most 25000 while others do so only if it costs above 75000” is not any more unrealistic than assuming that the proposer is indifferent between their project being approved for the minimum feasible amount and it not being approved at all. Honestly, the former seems plausible to me because people can consider the same project to have a different worth. Even if we agree this is unrealistic, one could study how the restriction that does not allow this behaves. This is naturally outside the scope of the project, but it could be discussed as a possible avenue of future work.

ANSWER: Thanks for this remark! Regarding the example against cost-interval games, our critique is that the broad possibility of setting approval ranges allows for quite implausible, unreasonably low, or unreasonably high selections.  We will discuss the direction you suggest in the final version of the paper! On the other hand, we view the indifference between a project being funded for the minimum feasible amount and it not being funded at all as a boundary condition.


QUESTIONS

1) Line 28: "This happens, e.g., ...": Without knowing more details, this sentence reads unconvincing. For instance, if the price of a project is too unrealistic, it would lose votes. Could you elaborate more why the rules you mentioned encourage submitting more expensive proposals?

Therefore, proposers of the most popular projects are incentivized to raise their price.  Indeed, while unrealistic prices may discourage the voters, we assume that together with the cost, the proposers also extend the scopes of their projects. Hence, the projects maintain reasonable cost given the scope. Notably, in Pabulib one can observe that more expensive projects tend to receive more votes than the cheap ones. REVIEWER'S COMMENTS   

1. At a high level, some of the positive results are unsurprising. For rules that iteratively build the winning slate and are insensitive to project cost, it makes perfect sense that each project should maximize its reported cost, conditioned on not 'falling off' of the end of the budget.

ANSWER: While some of the positive results may appear intuitive, omitting them would make the paper incomplete. Our positive results are used to showcase differences between voting rules, which in our view are not always obvious.

2. If strategic behavior is evident, why is it empirically so far from best response or equilibrium? If it is because of incomplete information in practice, are Nash equilibria the right way to model this phenomenon?

ANSWER: Some PB instances, for example the instances from Wroclaw, often follow the NE predicted for BasicAV. In other cities, proposers may also be taking into account various other considerations than simply maximizing project cost (such as their unwillingness to propose very large scale projects or their attitude towards public funds being spent efficiently). Finally, most PB instances in Pabulib employ the BasicAV rule, so we cannot hope to see equilibra for other rules, except for a few cases of MES-Cost. In this case, there were so few elections that employ MES that the voters might have simply not gotten to the point of understanding the rule sufficiently well to act in an optimal strategic way.

3. I found the notational choices somewhat confusing. Should $c(p_i)$ on line 173.5 in fact be $c_i$? If $c$ and $d$ are both project-dimensional cost vectors, why not make their `type' and notation symmetric?

ANSWER: Thank you for your suggestions, we will incorporate them in the final version!

4. I also found some of the technical language -- particularly the order of quantifiers -- around results relating to tie-breaking unclear. For instance, does (b) in the statement of Corollary 4.6 mean 'for all A/D TBOs' ... or 'there exists an A/D TBO...'? 

ANSWER: Thank you for this comment, we will make sure to clarify our technical language! In this particular case, Corollary 4.6(b) follows from Theorem 4.4., so we mean 'for all A/D TBOs'.

5. More discussion of why rules with PSNEs are normatively preferable would be helpful. This is especially true since the assumption that all votes are common knowledge is quite strong. When are these PSNEs such that they can be played without perfectly knowing all voters' approved projects beforehand?

ANSWER: We view the existence of a pure Nash equilibrium as a certain measure of predictability of the value towards which the cost might gravitate. Furthermore, it also provides an information about the qualities of particular voting rules, and incentives that they create for project proposers. For instance, we can observe that Method of Equal Shares promotes cheaper or more expensive projects depending on its variant, which gives us an additional information about benefits and consequences of applying the specific variant of the rule. In this sense, we view the NE analysis as the way of understanding PB rules, and their effect on project proposers' behaviour.

Furthermore, the amount of information regarding voters' preferences needed for strategic play is not equal among the voting rules. For instance, BasicAV or AV/Cost do not require knowledge about individual ballots. Instead, under them it is enough to know the sizes of particular projects' support sets, which is a much weaker requirement.


QUESTIONS

1) Why did you choose this particular form of proposer utility (line 173.5)? Since all rules are deterministic, this is a full-information setting, and you're after pure strategies, it seems like you might need only (i) that proposers are indifferent between being funded below the minimum and receiving no funding, and (ii) for c > d utility is monotonically increasing. Does this check out? If so, I think it strengthens the case for this model.

ANSWER: We believe that what the reviewer suggests is correct and generalizes our model. In our model a proposer would never submit a cost below the delivery one. This, in essence, translates to being indifferent between being funded below the minimum or not being funded at all, as in the reviewer's suggestion. The generalization follows from assuming an arbitrary monotonic increase of the utility when one gets funded. Our arguments, currently using a linear increase of utility, would remain valid for this case of strictly monotonic ones---the proposer wants as much money as possible to get and the specific rate of growth of the utility is not relevant (as long as the project remains funded). Thus, overall, both approaches are strategically equivalent.

2) In Section 6 and the discussion following Theorem 6.1, the more general model you contrast against seems to allow voters to have both different minimum and maximum thresholds for project costs, outside of which they will not vote for the project. An intermediate choice (and perhaps a more reasonable one for value-conscious voters) might be that they share a common minimum equal to the project's minimum cost, and have different maximum thresholds. Does Theorem 6.1 remain true in this intermediate model, or do some rules still admit PSNEs?

ANSWER: Thanks for this suggestion! First, it is worth observing that setting a common lower threshold for support is analogous to setting its delivery price (it is never profitable for a proposer to set the cost of a project below the threshold). The properties of this intermediate model are not obvious, so we cannot give precise information at the moment.


3) For what proportion of runs did your heuristic PSNE-finding algorithm fail to converge? For the rules where you do not prove there is a unique PSNE, did you find evidence of multiple distinct PSNEs? Multiple substantially different PSNEs?


ANSWER: Generally, we got a qualitatively the same result for every run of our heuristic and we did not observe evidence of nonunique PSNE. However, the computations rarely "fully converged" in the sense that often a small number of fairly cheap and not widely supported projects could still be funded if we decreased their cost by a tiny amount. We believe that we could reach full convergence if we dynamically adjusted the cost-change ranges, but we were satisfied with the qualitative results.

This submission concerns strategic aspects of project proposal in the standard model of approval-voting-based participatory budgeting. There are a number of standard preference aggregation rules -- drawn from both theory and practice -- which take in project (voter) approval sets and costs, along with an overall budget, and output a deterministic budget-feasible subset of projects (possibly making use of a prescribed tie-breaking rule or order). 

Atop this setting, the submission proposes a game-theoretic formulation of the process from the project proposer's perspective. Each project has a minimum cost (analogous to a reservation price), and proposers can specify a project cost above this minimum. If the project is funded, the proposer's utility is the difference between their specified cost and the minimum; if unfunded, then $0$. The task is then to establish for which combinations of rules, restricted approval profile settings, conditions on the minimum cost, and assumptions about the tie-breaking rule used this game has pure-strategy Nash equilibria (PSNEs), and what they are. 

The submission finally analyzes a few actual participatory budgeting instances, comparing the reported project costs to individually computed best response project costs according to the specified game. It also heuristically attempts to identify PSNEs in these instances, and compares the PSNE found with the reported costs in the profile.

summary.value:
The paper studies the following game-theoretical problem related to participatory budgeting (PB): 
The input consists of a PB instance with approval preferences where each project has a distinct proposer and minimum cost (delivery cost) and the proposers are the players such that the utility of a player is equal to the suggested cost minus the delivery cost if the  project is winning; otherwise the utility is zero.

The paper is interested in finding out whether there exits a strategy profile (i.e., cost per project that is at least the delivery cost) that is a Nash equilibrium for each some commonly studied PB rules.

The authors show the following
(1) For approval voting (AV) with a fixed tie-breaking order, there is an NE where the profile with the most approvals reports the whole budget as its cost and is the only winner. 

(2) For AV/Cost, i.e., approval voting where the approvals are divided by the project cost, they show that if the minimum delivery costs over all the projects are less than the budget, then all the projects are funded. More generally, a NE always exists for some tie-breaking rule. 

(3) Phragmén-rule may not admit a NE. 

(4)There is a polynomial-time algorithm that computes a near-unique NE for MES with cost utilities, whereas for MES with approval utilities, an NE may not exist.

(5) The authors show experimentally that under AV, the game converges to NE where the winner takes the whole budget. For AV/Cost, Phragmén, and MES with approval utilities, projects report costs that are proportional to their support, while MES with cost utilities has a few projects who report higher costs.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strength: The paper appears technically sound. The assumptions and setting are described clearly. The paper studies a quite interesting problem and presents an interesting angle for judging different PB rules. 

Weakness: It's not clear why the player's utility is precisely how much money the project additionally brings. For instance, it could be that the proposers care first and foremost about getting the project funded to the smallest feasible amount, and the extra money after that is far less important – so something akin to the extended utility function of Remark 3.1.

Secondly, the arguments against cost-interval games in PB (Section 6) sees not very convincing as well. summary.value:
This paper evaluates several Participatory Budgeting (PB) algorithms based on the equilibrium induced by these rules when strategic proposers act rationally. Authors also provide extensive experimental analysis on publicly available datasets. The important results in the paper are:

1) MES with cost utilities always admit a Pure Nash Equilibrium (PNE). The resultant project selection under this rule leads to a larger number of project approvals. 

 2) The BasicAV algorithm also admits PNE under which a single largest project is approved.  

3) Other rules, such as AV/Cost, Phragmen and  MES with approval utilities, do not guarantee PNE.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths: The paper is well written and easy to follow. The problem studied in the paper is rooted in real-world applications. Authors also do a commendable job in providing real-world instances of the settings studied in the paper. The mathematical analysis and experimental analysis are rigorous. 

Weaknesses: I do not find any significant flaws in the paper. However, intuitive explanations of some of the results in the paper will improve its readability, especially in Section 4.4. Further weaknesses include a lack of robustness analysis and a lack of practical relevance of the proposed solution in the real world.

questions.value:
1. I could not fully understand the end goal here. While equilibrium analysis in the paper is mostly predictive analysis, it will help if the authors comment on the prescriptive angle of the analysis as well. As a proposer deciding how to set project prices, what information do I need for different selection rules, and how realistic is it to obtain and/or process the information? 

2. Can authors comment on the rules that induce the desired equilibrium point in the Nash strategy (or dominant strategy) profile? In other words, do there exist mechanisms that induce the desired equilibrium outcome?

3. The paper lacks robustness studies. How robust are the equilibrium notions to miscalculation by a single or/few agents?

summary.value: This paper studies a "meta game" of participatory budgeting: when all the preference is known, what is a stable pricing for each alternatives if their makers are self-interested? It use a game theoretical approach to address this question and analyze equilibria under different participatory budgeting rules and restricted or general preferences domains. Results vary from case to case. For example, the most popular alternative takes all in BasicAV, while rules that emphasizes more on fairness (such as MES) may have more averaged equilibrium. There are also many negative results where a stable outcome does not exists. The paper also provides experiements that supports the theoretical findings.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strength:
The paper provides a very interesting perspective to examine PB mechanisms and games, different from the previous ones which focus on the vote itself. This inspires us to look into the problem more thoroughly. The theoretical characterizations are clean and complete, characterizing a wider range of common rules. I don't check most of the proofs, but some of them seem non-trivial to me. 

Weaknesses:
The paper indeed has many assumptions and restrictions in its modelling, which it also discusses in the introduction. I am generally satisfied with the second one (project do not affect approvals). Yet for the first one, I will expect more explanations. For example, it remains unclear to me whether a 100% percent sure Ground Truth versus a partial knowledge /noisy signal makes a different in the existence of equilibria.

questions.value:
1. How will exact ground truth / noisy information on voters' preferences affect the existence of an equilibrium? Do you at least have some guesses or conjectures?

2. In remark 2.1, you mentioned that you complement MES by Phragmen rules to use up the budget as much as possible. Will this complementary process affect the equilibrium?

3. In the second paragraph of the intro, there are sentences like "Among 25% instances, half of them XXX; in another 50%, more than 30% YYY". This kind of expression looks counterintuitive to me. Why not count the properties based on the whole dataset? 

4. I would like to hear more potential applications or insights this paper could give on future research or voting practices.

title.value: Strategic Cost Selection in Participatory Budgeting

abstract.value:
We study strategic behavior of project proposers in the context of approval-based
participatory budgeting (PB). In our model we assume that the votes are fixed and
known and the proposers want to set as high project prices as possible, provided
that their projects get selected and the prices are not below the minimum costs of
their delivery. We study the existence of pure Nash equilibria (NE) in such games,
focusing on the AV/Cost, Phragmen, and Method of Equal Shares rules. We also
provide an experimental study of cost selection on real-life PB election data.

The PC Chairs will analyze aggregated data to understand how emerging technologies influence the research publication process. Please select all that apply below.
